title: Half of Texas's 474 GW Data Center Queue Won't Survive This Audit. Will Yours?
summary: Texas paused all 474 GW of data center requests in the ERCOT queue pending a PUCT audit. What the audit requires and how to prove your project is real.
body_markdown:
> **Update, October 29, 2026:** ERCOT now expects to complete the audit around December 10, 2026. On September 21, Governor Abbott went further and[directed the TCEQ to halt all permits sought by data center projects](https://gov.texas.gov/news/post/governor-abbott-directs-tceq-to-halt-data-center-permits) until the ERCOT and Texas Water Development Board audits are complete, including for projects that are not in the interconnection queue.


## **What Texas ordered**


On August 3, Governor Abbott[directed the Public Utility Commission of Texas and ERCOT](https://www.texastribune.org/2026/08/03/texas-data-center-project-audit-greg-abbott/) to halt every data center project in the interconnection queue until a full audit is complete. This is functionally a moratorium and at Paces we are counting it as that until there is greater clarity.


This order affects 474 GW of ERCOT interconnection requests or more than five times the state's record peak demand. ~90% of it is data centers, and Paces customers have a meaningful share of it in their pipelines.


The direct damage to specific Texas project timelines is bad, but there are even larger concerns coming. You now have functional freezes in a very blue state (NY) and a very red state (TX), the two biggest development markets in the country. That is a permission structure for many of the state level legislatures to move existing data center moratoria bills forward. My honest expectation is that twelve months from now you see more than ten states that are currently highly active data center markets with some form of moratorium. Texas was the state that was never supposed to be on that list.


Texas's read is not entirely wrong; you can't run a grid on unverified, speculative load. It is very unfortunate how sudden this is, but every project now has to prove it's real to keep its place in line.


## **Why community impact is now the top site-screening criterion**


I wrote in[February](https://www.paces.com/post/the-98b-warning-power-ready-isnt-shovel-ready) that clearing the power bar went from the most important part of data center development to table stakes. We are now seeing that the emergent constraint on development is community impact. We've been tracking this nationwide. The pattern is consistent: local sentiment has become the number one site-screening criterion for our customers, ahead of power availability, for the first time.


## **What the audit requires**


PUCT and ERCOT now have to collect this on every project in queue:


- Projected power consumption and any on-site generation plans
- Projected water consumption and cooling technology
- Noise and setback mitigation
- Every tax incentive and abatement, received or expected
- Who actually owns the project


It is likely that most of that 474 GW never makes it through the audit. Not because the projects are bad. Because they were never real; they were filed to hold a queue position, not to build. The developers with financing, site control, and real water and community answers already in hand will clear this in weeks. Everyone else is about to find out how speculative their pipeline actually was.


## **How to prepare an ERCOT pipeline for the audit**


**Our approach at Paces is that power, permitting and other risks need to run in parallel, not sequentially. Texas has made the approach more necessary than ever.**


We’ve spent the past several months building directly into this gap.


- **Water Access** maps the providers serving a site: their supply, capacity, and constraints. You know whether the water a project needs actually exists before you commit capital.
- **Water Outreach** goes further. It engages the utilities and districts directly to confirm capacity and willingness to serve. Real documented evidence, not a guess about the aquifer.
- **Sensitive Receptors** , one of the newest modules on the platform, flags every school, hospital, and church within a kilometer of a site. You know your exposure before the first public meeting.
- **Regulatory Pathways and Permitting Matrix** maps every permit a project needs, jurisdiction by jurisdiction. The paperwork trail exists before a regulator asks for it.


None of this is a Texas-specific fix. It's the same diligence New York, Arizona, and Illinois are already asking for, just in different forms. More states will follow before the year is out.

If you agree or disagree with any of this, reach out to me on[LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jamesmcwalter/) .


## **Frequently Asked Questions**


### **What does the Texas data center queue audit require?**


PUCT and ERCOT are collecting, for every project in the queue, projected power consumption and on-site generation plans, projected water use and cooling technology, noise and setback mitigation, tax incentives received or expected, and project ownership.


### **Which Texas data center projects are likely to clear the audit?**


Projects with financing, site control, and documented answers on water supply and community impact already in hand. Speculative requests filed mainly to hold a queue position are the most exposed.


### **When will the Texas data center audit be complete?**


As of late October 2026, ERCOT expects to complete the audit around December 10, 2026. Until then, the Governor has also directed the TCEQ not to issue permits sought by data center projects.
